social.title: Mughal-Period Land, Revenue and Agrarian Society
social.part: Part Vii — Early Modern And Colonial Economic Transformations
social.summary: Mughal rule did not replace the agrarian society of Mithila, Vajji and Anga with a single uniform land system. It superimposed imperial fiscal claims, assignments and administrative categories upon village production, regional chieftaincies, hereditary local offices and ecologies shaped by the Ganga, Gandak, Kosi and their tributaries. The most useful contemporary source, Abu’l-Fazl’s A’in-i Akbari, gives unusually detailed fiscal statistics for the Bihar subah, including the sarkars of Tirhut, Hajipur and Munger. Yet those figures record assessed revenue and administrative knowledge; they do not by themselves tell us what every cultivator paid, what every zamindar retained, or how much was actually collected in a flood-prone year. This chapter therefore reconstructs Mughal agrarian society through a layered method: official statistics, regional revenue documents, the history of Bihar’s zamindars and chieftains, agrarian ecology, and later gazetteer summaries are used together but never treated as interchangeable archives. social.title: Trade between Bengal, Bihar, Nepal and the Gangetic World
social.part: Part Vii — Early Modern And Colonial Economic Transformations
social.summary: Trade connected the socio-economic worlds of Mithila, Vajji and Anga to regions far beyond their political boundaries. The Ganga formed the principal east–west trunk between the upper Gangetic plain and Bengal; Patna developed as a major inland entrepôt; Munger and Bhagalpur lay on the eastern river corridor; Hajipur and Tirhut fed northward routes toward Nepal; and Kathmandu connected plains commerce with Himalayan and Tibetan exchange. These links were already visible before European companies became major actors, then intensified and changed as English and Dutch merchants entered Bihar’s commodity markets. The evidence, however, is uneven. A late-sixteenth-century traveller, a seventeenth-century factory letter, a 1790s diplomatic mission and Buchanan-Hamilton’s early-nineteenth-century trade account cannot be collapsed into one timeless picture. This chapter therefore reconstructs circulation through securely dated layers: routes, transport, merchants, credit, commodities and market nodes are compared across sources while each observation remains tied to its own period. social.title: East India Company Expansion and the Remaking of Agrarian Relations
social.part: Part Vii — Early Modern And Colonial Economic Transformations
social.summary: Between the military victories of the East India Company in the 1750s and 1760s and the Permanent Settlement of 1793 lay nearly three decades of experimentation. The decisive change was not that a wholly new agrarian order appeared overnight after Plassey or Buxar. Rather, a commercial corporation acquired political leverage, then fiscal sovereignty, and gradually inserted its own supervisors, councils, collectors, auctions, revenue farmers, courts and accounting practices into an older Mughal–Nawabi system of zamindars, amils, qanungos, patwaris and village producers. Bihar is especially revealing because the transition can be seen through Shitab Rai’s revenue administration, the Patna Revenue Council, early experiments in Tirhut, the Rajmahal–Bhagalpur supervisory system and the uneven fiscal geography of Monghyr. This chapter follows that transition from 1757 to the eve of the Permanent Settlement. It therefore stops short of treating the 1793 settlement itself in detail; that belongs to Chapter 55. social.title: Permanent Settlement and Landed Society
social.part: Part Vii — Early Modern And Colonial Economic Transformations
social.summary: The Permanent Settlement of 1793 converted the experimental decennial settlement of Bengal and Bihar into a perpetual state demand upon designated zamindars, independent talukdars and other proprietors. Its importance lay not simply in fixing revenue, but in reworking the legal language of landed authority. A hereditary revenue-collecting right was increasingly treated as proprietary property, while punctual payment to the colonial state became the condition of security. Yet the settlement did not define every right below the zamindar. Raiyats, under-tenure holders, village officials, service tenures, rent-free grants and customary users continued to inhabit a layered agrarian field that subsequent regulations, courts and tenancy statutes tried to order. social.title: Indigo and Commercial Agriculture
social.part: Part Vii — Early Modern And Colonial Economic Transformations
social.summary: Indigo was one of the clearest ways in which colonial commercial agriculture entered the agrarian society created under permanent settlement. The crop linked cultivators and labourers in Bihar to European capital, Calcutta agency houses, factory processing, long-distance transport and volatile international dye markets. Yet the system was not uniform. Indigo could be grown directly on factory-controlled land, by tenants under advance-and-contract arrangements, or by independent cultivators. North Bihar—especially Tirhut, Darbhanga, Muzaffarpur, Saran and Champaran—became the principal European indigo zone during the nineteenth century, while Bhagalpur and Monghyr also supported significant production. This chapter therefore treats indigo as both a crop and an agrarian institution: it altered land use, credit, labour, rents, contracts and the distribution of risk. It also traces the technological and market crisis created by synthetic indigo after 1897 and the distinct Champaran conflict that culminated in the 1917 inquiry and the Champaran Agrarian Act of 1918. social.title: Opium and Other Commodity Networks

social.title: Famines, Scarcity and Food Security
social.part: Part Vii — Early Modern And Colonial Economic Transformations
social.summary: Scarcity has repeatedly exposed the relationship between ecology, markets, household resources and public authority in Mithila, Vajji and Anga. A failed monsoon or damaged rice crop could begin a crisis, but famine emerged only when households lost effective access to food: grain prices rose faster than wages, cattle and tools were sold, seed was eaten, credit contracted, employment failed, or transport could not move food from surplus to deficit areas. In 1769–70 severe drought interacted with Company revenue extraction, grain procurement, weak relief and epidemic disease to produce catastrophic mortality in Bihar. social.title: Colonial Surveys and the Invention of Social Categories
social.part: Part Vii — Early Modern And Colonial Economic Transformations
social.summary: Colonial surveys created an extraordinarily dense archive for the social history of Mithila, Vajji and Anga, but the archive must be read as a history of classification as well as a description of society. The central method of this chapter is chronological: a colonial category is evidence first for the date and administrative purpose in which it appears. It cannot be projected backward without independent period evidence. Colonial rule generated an expanding demand to describe the people it taxed, policed, recruited, litigated with and governed. The resulting surveys were never neutral inventories. Their headings reflected administrative problems: landholding, occupation, religion, language, “tribe,” “caste,” custom and rank. Yet it is equally misleading to treat every category as a pure colonial fabrication. social.title: Education under Colonialism
social.part: Part Vii — Early Modern And Colonial Economic Transformations
social.summary: Colonial education transformed the institutional ecology of Mithila, Vajji and Anga by linking schools, examinations and credentials to a growing public and professional labour market. The change was cumulative rather than substitutive. Sanskrit ṭols, vernacular schools, maktabs, madrasas and household learning persisted while government schools, aided institutions, colleges and university examinations expanded. This chapter traces that layered transition from the early nineteenth-century surveys to Patna University in 1917, with special attention to language, access, patronage, gender and the economic value of credentials. Education under colonialism did not begin with an empty landscape and did not proceed as a single replacement of “traditional” learning by English schools. Mithila, Vajji and Anga already contained Sanskrit scholarly institutions, elementary schools, maktabs, madrasas, household teaching and occupational transmission. The colonial period added new layers: government schools, inspection, grants-in-aid, prescribed curricula, public examinations, colleges and eventually a regional university. social.title: Print Culture
social.part: Part Vii — Early Modern And Colonial Economic Transformations
social.summary: Print culture changed the social life of texts in Mithila, Vajji and Anga by making arguments, reports, literary works and linguistic claims reproducible across distance. It did not erase manuscript or oral transmission. social.title: Railways, Roads and Changing Markets
social.part: Part Vii — Early Modern And Colonial Economic Transformations
social.summary: Railways reorganized the economic geography of Mithila, Vajji and Anga without erasing rivers, roads, ferries or animal transport. South of the Ganga, the East Indian Railway reached major Anga towns in the early 1860s; north of the river, the Tirhut network expanded from famine-relief construction in the 1870s into a branching metre-gauge system. Stations and junctions changed market hierarchy, roads increasingly became railway feeders, and new links drew frontier trade toward railheads. At the same time, flood ecology, river crossings, gauge breaks and the continuing need for carts preserved substantial friction. This chapter reconstructs that layered transport economy and treats market integration as an uneven historical process rather than an automatic result of railway mileage. Colonial transport history in Mithila, Vajji and Anga cannot be reduced to a sequence in which railways arrived and older routes vanished. Before rail construction, the Ganga and its tributaries, ferries, seasonal roads, carts, pack animals and foot traffic already connected village production to market towns and longer-distance commerce. social.title: Labour Migration
social.part: Part Vii — Early Modern And Colonial Economic Transformations
social.summary: Labour migration became one of the most consequential connections between the agrarian households of Mithila, Vajji and Anga and the expanding colonial economy. Yet there was no single migrant stream. Seasonal workers, circular urban migrants, railway and workshop labourers, plantation recruits, women moving within family labour strategies, and indentured emigrants faced different destinations and different degrees of freedom. Railways lowered travel frictions, but recruitment networks and labour law often determined whether movement remained reversible. This chapter reconstructs those differentiated circuits while keeping census categories, household strategies and coercive labour regimes analytically distinct. Colonial labour migration from Mithila, Vajji and Anga took several forms that must be kept analytically separate. Some cultivators and labourers left for a few weeks or months during slack agricultural seasons; others worked repeatedly in Calcutta, Howrah or railway centres while maintaining a village household; some moved with families to plantation zones; and a much smaller share entered overseas indenture. social.title: Women and Colonial Modernity
social.part: Part Vii — Early Modern And Colonial Economic Transformations
social.summary: Colonial modernity altered women’s lives in Mithila, Vajji and Anga through schools, law, print, medicine, labour markets, migration and nationalist politics, but the changes were profoundly unequal. Female literacy remained low even as girls’ education became an explicit field of policy; statutes changed the legal treatment of widow remarriage, consent and child marriage without ensuring uniform social compliance; hospitals and trained female personnel expanded without displacing household medicine; and political mobilisation made women publicly visible while leaving the economic weight of unpaid labour poorly recorded. This chapter reconstructs those layered transformations while treating the silences of the colonial archive as part of the history itself. Women in Mithila, Vajji and Anga encountered colonial modernity not as a single transition from an old social order to a new one, but through overlapping institutions that moved at different speeds. social.title: The Historical India–Nepal Borderland Economy
social.part: Part Viii — Nepal Mithila / Madhesh As A Social And Economic Region
social.summary: The India–Nepal boundary across Mithila and the wider eastern Tarai/Madhesh did not create two self-contained economies. From the late eighteenth century onward, Gorkha consolidation, Company expansion, the Anglo–Gorkha War, boundary demarcation, customs administration and railway construction altered the terms of movement without abolishing the economic continuities of the plains. This chapter therefore treats the border as an institution embedded in a corridor: politically real, fiscally consequential and increasingly surveyed, yet continually crossed by commodities, labour, credit, kinship and pilgrimage. The historical economy joining north Bihar to the Nepal Tarai and the Himalayan interior was older than the modern boundary. River systems, alluvial plains, forest belts and foothill passes produced a north–south gradient of exchange. A single field could carry several distinct relationships at once: the state might claim land revenue; a grantee might receive that revenue under birta or another assignment; a village intermediary might collect dues; and an actual cultivator might hold occupancy, tenancy or customary claims. The plains already contained towns, cultivated belts, forests, grazing grounds, pilgrimage routes and long-established Madhesi, Tharu and other communities. What changed rapidly was the relationship among disease ecology, forest access, state resettlement, spontaneous migration, roads, land law and agricultural expansion. This chapter reconstructs those linked processes, with particular attention to the eastern and central Tarai and to the Mithila/Madhesh districts, while using Chitwan and other Inner-Tarai projects only where they illuminate national policy rather than as substitutes for the regional history of Dhanusha, Mahottari, Sarlahi, Siraha and Saptari. Malaria control altered the cost and risk of permanent residence in lowland Nepal, but it did not by itself determine who migrated, where forest was cleared, or who gained land. Hill land pressure, state revenue goals, resettlement schemes, transport, cadastral administration, local labour demand, cross-border kinship and the availability of cultivable land all mattered. social.title: Migration and Settlement
social.part: Part Viii — Nepal Mithila / Madhesh As A Social And Economic Region
social.summary: Migration and settlement transformed the Nepal Tarai/Madhesh after the middle of the twentieth century, but neither process began in an empty landscape. The plains already contained long-established villages, market towns, pilgrimage centres, cultivated tracts, forests and grazing zones linked across the India–Nepal border. What changed after the 1950s was the scale, direction and institutional framing of movement. Malaria control reduced one environmental barrier; roads and markets lowered transport costs; land policy and resettlement programmes created new opportunities; and population pressure in the hills encouraged movement toward the lowlands. Migration records movement from one place to another; settlement concerns the establishment of residence, cultivation, property claims and social institutions. social.title: Language, Education and Cultural Institutions in Nepal
social.part: Part Viii — Nepal Mithila / Madhesh As A Social And Economic Region
social.summary: Language, education and cultural institutions in Nepal Mithila/Madhesh have never formed a single hierarchy. Maithili has long been a language of household life, ritual, literature, performance and cross-border communication, while Sanskrit, Nepali, Hindi, Urdu, Bhojpuri, Bajjika and English have occupied different institutional niches at different times. The modern state expanded schools, examinations, universities, academies and broadcasting, but it also attached unequal prestige and administrative power to languages. The historical problem is therefore not whether Maithili survived, but how institutions distributed literacy, credentials, public visibility and cultural authority among languages. This chapter treats language policy, schooling and cultural organisation together because each changed the social value of the others. The eastern and central Tarai/Madhesh were multilingual before mass schooling. Maithili dominated large parts of Saptari, Siraha, Dhanusha and Mahottari, but speech communities interacted with Bhojpuri, Bajjika, Urdu, Nepali, Sanskrit and Hindi through markets, courts, pilgrimage, marriage and religious instruction. social.part: Part Viii — Nepal Mithila / Madhesh As A Social And Economic Region
social.summary: Gender, citizenship and household economy meet most visibly where formal rights encounter everyday dependence. In Nepal Mithila/Madhesh, women’s economic position has been shaped not only by wages and land but also by marriage, migration, unpaid care, civil-registration documents, inheritance practice, access to schooling and the ability to move between household, market and public office. This chapter therefore treats citizenship as an economic institution as well as a legal status, while distinguishing constitutional rights, statutory pathways and their uneven implementation in households and local administrations. Most production and welfare in Madhesh pass through households before they appear in markets or state statistics. social.title: Janakpur Art, Crafts and Cultural Economy
social.part: Part Viii — Nepal Mithila / Madhesh As A Social And Economic Region
social.summary: Janakpur’s cultural economy is not simply a market for paintings. It joins ritual practice, women’s domestic knowledge, portable art, craft production, pilgrimage, tourism, institutional development, public murals, training, galleries, collectors and digital circulation. The same motif can move from a wedding wall to handmade paper, from a household threshold to a textile, ceramic object or urban mural, and from a devotional setting to a tourist purchase. Such movement changes scale, materials, authorship and price, but it does not automatically sever the work from Mithila’s ritual and social worlds. This chapter therefore treats art and craft as economic activities embedded in living cultural institutions rather than as detached commodities. A cultural economy includes the labour that creates an object, the knowledge that makes it intelligible, the institutions that certify and circulate it, and the places and events that attract buyers. social.title: Border Markets, Remittances and Informal Exchange
social.part: Part Viii — Nepal Mithila / Madhesh As A Social And Economic Region
social.summary: The India–Nepal border economy of Madhesh is neither wholly formal nor wholly informal. It is a layered system in which kinship travel, weekly markets, petty retail, commercial customs trade, labour mobility, remittance transfers, currency exchange and digital payments coexist. A person may cross the border legally without immigration formalities while the goods carried remain subject to customs rules. A household may receive a bank remittance from the Gulf, hand-carried earnings from India and commodities bought in a Bihar market during the same month. This chapter therefore separates movement of people, goods and money before asking how they interact. It also treats unrecorded exchange as an empirical category rather than automatically equating it with criminal trafficking.
